finding: shop/migrations/0006_safe.py:12 The RunSQL sets slug = '' for NULL rows and has only a no-op reverse, so the data change is irreversible. It also sits next to a RunPython whose forward function does nothing. Rolling back with migrate shop 0005 leaves every previously NULL slug as '' with no way to restore the original NULLs. A later unique constraint on slug would then collide on the empty strings. The same irreversibility applies to the active backfill in 0007 line 15.

alembic/versions/3b1f_add_refunds.py:18 The downgrade runs DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY in the same transaction, which PostgreSQL rejects. The statement order also leaves a half-done downgrade. alembic downgrade 2a0e fails on the DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY line with the same transaction-block error, so the rollback cannot complete. The reason column drop runs first. If the migration were not transactional, this would leave a partly rolled-back schema. Wrap the drop in autocommit_block, or use a plain DROP INDEX.

db/migrations/0002_orders.sql:2 Both SQL migrations have no down step and are not marked one-way. db/migrations/0001_safe.sql and 0002_orders.sql contain only forward statements (add column, index, constraints). No down section, no paired down file, and no comment saying the migration is one-way. The alembic and Django migrations in the same change do ship reverse steps. 0002 is deployed and the FK validation or the new index causes trouble in production. To roll back, an operator has to hand-write DROP CONSTRAINT orders_customer_fk, DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY orders_customer_idx and DROP COLUMN tracking_code under pressure. If 0002 failed part-way, nothing in the repo says which statements already committed, since CONCURRENTLY statements cannot sit in a rollback-able transaction.

alembic/versions/3b1f_add_refunds.py:12 CREATE/DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY runs inside Alembic's default migration transaction and fails. 3b1f_add_refunds.py:12 (upgrade) and :18 (downgrade, DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY) call op.execute directly. There is no op.get_context().autocommit_block() and no env.py in the tree that sets transaction_per_migration off or autocommit. On PostgreSQL Alembic wraps each migration in a transaction by default, and PostgreSQL rejects CONCURRENTLY there. db/migrations/0001_safe.sql:9 CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY sits in a multi-statement file, which most SQL migration runners execute as one transaction (psql -1, Flyway, golang-migrate multi-statement), and PostgreSQL rejects it there. The runner wraps the file in a transaction, or sends it as one multi-statement simple query. The index statement errors, and either the whole migration rolls back or the index is never built. It needs its own non-transactional migration file or runner directive. The same applies to 0002_orders.sql line 4.
shop/migrations/0006_safe.py (line 10) has the same problem. It depends on ("shop", "0005_initial"), and main has no shop migrations at all.

shop/migrations/0007_backfill.py:7 The backfill loads every product and calls save() one at a time (N+1 writes), and it ignores the unique and NULL cases. On a large shop_product table, this is one UPDATE per row inside a single migration transaction, which is slow and holds locks the whole time. A single Product.objects.filter(slug='').update(slug=Cast('pk', CharField())) would do the same job. Because save() is called without update_fields, it can also overwrite concurrent changes to other columns.

shop/migrations/0007_backfill.py:6 Backfill saves one row at a time and runs with an unbatched UPDATE, all in a single transaction. fill_slugs loads every matching Product and calls p.save() per row (lines 6-8): one SELECT then N UPDATEs, each saving every field. The RunSQL at line 15 is an unbounded UPDATE shop_product SET active = true WHERE active IS NULL. The migration is atomic by default on PostgreSQL, so row locks from the Python loop and the SQL update are held until the end of the whole migration. Production shop_product has 5 million rows with empty slug. The migration issues 5 million single-row UPDATEs inside one transaction, locks each row until commit, and any checkout write to those products blocks or deadlocks for the duration. A failure near the end rolls everything back and wastes the run.

db/migrations/0002_orders.sql:7 The foreign key is added NOT VALID and validated in the same script. Run as one transaction, it keeps a SHARE ROW EXCLUSIVE lock on both orders and customers during validation. Writes to orders and customers block while validation scans orders. If any order has an orphaned customer_id, the validation fails and rolls back the whole migration, including the tracking_code column and the index. Split it into two migrations.

shop/migrations/0007_backfill.py:8 Backfill saves every column of each product row, so it can overwrite concurrent updates, and runs row by row in one transaction. fill_slugs lines 6-8 loads every Product with slug="" through the historical model, then calls p.save() with no update_fields. Django's save() writes all fields from the in-memory copy. Django migrations on PostgreSQL are atomic by default, so the loop is one long transaction and it takes row locks as it goes. The app keeps serving during the deploy (the point of an expand/backfill step). Product 42 has slug="". The migration loads it, then an admin changes its price or stock. The migration reaches p.save() and writes the old price and stock back with the slug. The admin's edit is lost with no error. On a large catalogue, N separate UPDATEs make this window long and hold row locks until the final commit, so concurrent writers to those rows block.

db/migrations/0001_safe.sql:12 ADD CONSTRAINT ... NOT VALID is followed by VALIDATE CONSTRAINT in the same file. Run as one transaction, the ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock from the ADD is held through the validation scan. On a large orders table, the migration holds an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock for the whole validation scan. That blocks all reads and writes, which is the outage NOT VALID is meant to avoid. VALIDATE should go in a separate migration or transaction. The validation will also fail outright if any existing row has total <= 0.

db/migrations/0002_orders.sql:6 NOT VALID and VALIDATE sit in the same file as CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY, so no runner can honour both. 0002 mixes CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY (line 4), which must run outside a transaction, with ADD CONSTRAINT ... NOT VALID (line 6) and VALIDATE CONSTRAINT (line 7), which only avoid a long lock if they commit separately. 0001 lines 9, 12 and 13 do the same. No runner or config is in the repo to show the file is split per statement. If the runner sends the file as one batch or one transaction, CONCURRENTLY fails. If the runner wraps it in a transaction while skipping the CONCURRENTLY check, ADD CONSTRAINT keeps its lock (SHARE ROW EXCLUSIVE on orders and customers) through the full-table scan in VALIDATE, which undoes the point of NOT VALID. A runner that applies a .sql file as a single multi-statement query (a psycopg2 execute of the whole text, or a Flyway or sqitch transactional mode) turns the file into an implicit transaction: line 4 raises CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY cannot run inside a transaction block and nothing after it applies. A runner in autocommit mode applies it, but the runner has to be one that nothing in this change names.
